items.readable_text:
Content:
In the diagram below, [MATH: \triangle ABC] is inscribed in a circle with center [MATH: O.] This means that all three of the triangle's vertices lie on the circle's circumference.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6211fa4c51ee009df2576ac4510d3488]

Content:
From the diagram, we can see that [MATH: \overline{AB}] passes through the point [MATH: O.] So, [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter of the circle.

Content:
Based on this information, Thales' theorem tells us that the triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] must be a right triangle. More precisely:

Content:
> If [MATH: A, B,] and [MATH: C] are distinct points on a circle where [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter, then [MATH: m\angle C = 90^\circ.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cfe2fee8c6bb56587e64a9bb83246a08]

Content:
Now that we know [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a right triangle, we can apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the length of the hypotenuse:

Content:
[MATH: AB|= sqrt(AC^{2} + BC^{2}); = sqrt(8^{2} + 6^{2}); = sqrt(64 + 36); = sqrt(100); = 10cm]

items.title: Finding the Radius of a Circle Given an Inscribed Right Triangle

sections.normalized_html: Consider the figure below, where [MATH: AC=7\,\textrm{cm}] and [MATH: BC=24\,\textrm{cm}.] What is the radius of the circle?
sections.readable_text:
Consider the figure below, where [MATH: AC=7\,\textrm{cm}] and [MATH: BC=24\,\textrm{cm}.] What is the radius of the circle?

[IMG: /graphics/fe89aca96133297aa49b60959d0feab8]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] is inscribed in the circle, where the side [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter. Therefore, [MATH: m\angle{ACB}=90^\circ.]

So, by the Pythagorean theorem, we have [MATH: AB|= sqrt(AC^{2} + BC^{2}); = sqrt(7^{2} + 24^{2}); = sqrt(625); = 25cm.]

Finally, the radius of the circle is [MATH: OA = \dfrac{AB}{2} = \dfrac{25}{2} = 12.5 \,\textrm{cm}.]

sections.normalized_html: The radius of the above circle is [MATH: 10\,\textrm{m}] and [MATH: AC=12\,\textrm{m}.] What is the length of the chord [MATH: \overline{BC}?]

The radius of the above circle is [MATH: 10\,\textrm{m}] and [MATH: AC=12\,\textrm{m}.] What is the length of the chord [MATH: \overline{BC}?]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle{ACB}] is inscribed in the circle, where [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter. Therefore, by Thales' theorem, we have that [MATH: m\angle{C}=90^\circ,] as shown below.

Now, [MATH: AB=2AO=2 \cdot 10 = 20 \, \textrm{m}.]

Finally, by the Pythagorean theorem, [MATH: BC^{2}|= AB^{2} − AC^{2}; = 20^{2} − 12^{2}; = 400 − 144; = 256.]

So, [MATH: BC = \sqrt{256} = 16\,\textrm{cm}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In the diagram below, [MATH: \triangle ABC] is inscribed in a circle with center [MATH: O.] This means that all three of the triangle's vertices lie on the circle's circumference.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6211fa4c51ee009df2576ac4510d3488]

Content:
From the diagram, we can see that [MATH: \overline{AB}] passes through the point [MATH: O.] So, [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter of the circle.

Content:
Based on this information, Thales' theorem tells us that the triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC] must be a right triangle. More precisely:

Content:
> If [MATH: A, B,] and [MATH: C] are distinct points on a circle where [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter, then [MATH: m\angle C = 90^\circ.]

Content:
Now that we know [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a right triangle, we can apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the length of the hypotenuse:

Content:
[MATH: AB|= sqrt(AC^{2} + BC^{2}); = sqrt(8^{2} + 6^{2}); = sqrt(64 + 36); = sqrt(100); = 10cm]
